questions.question: Why does an indefinite integral include $+C$?

Because all antiderivatives differ by an additive constant.
Because differentiation removes the variable, under all circumstances whatsoever.
questions.explanation: All antiderivatives of $f$ differ by an additive constant (since differentiation annihilates constants), so the indefinite integral is the family $F(x)+C$.

questions.question: Which statement avoids a common misunderstanding about indefinite integrals?
options: An indefinite integral is a family of functions, not a single numerical value.
An indefinite integral always has fixed endpoints.
An indefinite integral is always divergent.
An indefinite integral is the same as a horizontal asymptote.
questions.explanation: Without bounds the symbol represents functions $F+C$, not one numerical area.
questions.source_support: The interpretation says an indefinite integral describes a family rather than a single numerical value.
option_explanations: Fixed endpoints characterize definite integrals.
Indefinite integrals are not convergence claims.

A horizontal asymptote is a tail-behaviour statement $\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}f(x)=L$, describing a line a function approaches; an indefinite integral $\int f\,\mathrm{d}x=F+C$ is the family of antiderivatives, with no bounds or limiting direction involved.

questions.question: If two functions are both antiderivatives of the same function $f$, how are they related in this context?
options: They differ only by a constant.
They must be identical at every point.
questions.explanation: On an interval, if $F'=G'=f$, then $(F-G)'=0$, so $F-G$ is constant; the two antiderivatives differ only by a constant.

Their derivatives are the same (both equal $f$); having the same derivative is what makes both antiderivatives, not different derivatives.
Both can be antiderivatives; e.g. $x^2$ and $x^2+5$ are both antiderivatives of $2x$, so the claim 'cannot both' is false.
